8efda60d4f.q: Why did OneLaw start building a legal practice management system to replace LawBase?
8efda60d4f.a: When CCH sold LawBase to LexisNexis, the new owner realized they had acquired a product with a Visual Basic 6 codebase that had no easy path forward into the Microsoft.net world. They announced its retirement and wanted to replace it with an Australian product, but many New Zealand law firms that Doug was consulting with did not like the replacement product or anything else on the market at the time. Since LawBase had approximately 630 firms and represented the lion's share of the mid-market, Doug saw this as an opportunity to start OneLaw.

d99ed3394c.q: What is the combined ledger trust account system that protects New Zealand legal software from international competition?
d99ed3394c.a: New Zealand operates a combined ledger trust account system that is different from every other country on the planet except for Scotland. This unique accounting approach for handling client trust funds means that international legal software providers cannot easily adapt their systems to work in New Zealand, creating natural protection from competition but also limiting OneLaw's appeal in other markets.

6ec11d75d5.a: OneLaw's first line of code was written in May 2009, and the minimum viable product was completed by mid-2012, taking approximately three years—two years longer than originally anticipated and costing significantly more money than expected. 12ee1dacb5.q: What incident in Penang revealed why CCH's LawBase expansion into Malaysia failed?
12ee1dacb5.a: During a product demonstration to a law firm in Penang, the chief partner asked if he could have two copies of the system—one for the auditors and another for what was actually happening with the money. This revealed that the market did not want to comply with a compliance product, exposing a fundamental business model problem. Doug immediately reported this finding to his boss Matthew Sullivan in Singapore, and they decided to exit Malaysia by the end of 2005, having sold only eight or nine systems.

5699a52922.q: How did OneLaw acquire its first customers in Christchurch after the 2011 earthquake?
5699a52922.a: After the February 2011 Christchurch earthquake, most law firms in the city were focused on finding new premises rather than changing their practice management system. Doug discovered through a contact that two firms—Ian McNeish in Kaia Poi and Williams McKenzie in Rangiora—had purchased LawBase six months before its retirement announcement. He offered them OneLaw for free as a trial in exchange for protecting their LawBase investment, and both agreed. Both firms remained customers, with Ian McNeish's business eventually rolling into Pegasus Bay Law.

1051833ead.q: How did OneLaw grow its customer base in New Zealand through referral rather than advertising?
1051833ead.a: OneLaw did not need to spend money on advertising because the New Zealand legal community is small and tight-knit, with lawyers being very collegial. As long as OneLaw delivered good installations and made customers happy, those customers would talk about the product to others. This referral-based growth strategy was enabled by the interconnected nature of the legal profession in New Zealand, where lawyers discuss management ideas and practices with each other regularly.
